top_level_objectives: Understand that electron pairs (domains) around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
Differentiate between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Predict the electron-domain and molecular geometries for molecules with 2 to 6 electron domains.
Explain how lone pairs influence molecular geometry and bond angles compared to bonding pairs.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron domains repel each other and will arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
key_visuals: A central sphere representing an atom.
Abstract 'electron domain' objects that can be attached to the central sphere.
Visual repulsion forces (e.g., glowing lines) appearing between domains when they are close.
student_actions: Place two electron domains on a central atom and observe them snap into a linear arrangement.
Add a third domain and watch the three domains form a trigonal planar geometry.
Add a fourth domain and see the structure dynamically shift into a tetrahedral shape.

scenes.scene_name: Electron vs. Molecular Geometry: The Tetrahedral Family
scenes.brief_purpose: To distinguish between the arrangement of all electron domains (electron geometry) and the arrangement of only the atoms (molecular geometry), using the 4-domain family as an example.
key_visuals: A 3D model of methane (CH4) with its tetrahedral shape highlighted.
A 3D model of ammonia (NH3) with its lone pair shown as a translucent cloud.
A 3D model of water (H2O) with its two lone pairs shown as clouds.
Labels indicating 'Electron Geometry: Tetrahedral' for all three molecules, but different 'Molecular Geometry' labels (Tetrahedral, Trigonal Pyramidal, Bent).
student_actions: Start with a methane model (4 bonding domains).
Tap a bonding domain to convert it into a lone pair, observing the molecule morph into ammonia's trigonal pyramidal shape.
Convert another bonding domain to a lone pair, watching the model become the bent shape of water.
Toggle the visibility of the lone pair clouds to see how the molecular shape is defined only by the atoms.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pair Repulsion and Bond Angles
scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate why lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, causing deviations from ideal bond angles.
key_visuals: A model of methane showing the ideal 109.5° bond angle.
A model of water with larger, more diffuse lone pair clouds and a compressed 104.5° bond angle.
An animation showing the larger lone pair clouds 'pushing' the bonding pairs closer together.
student_actions: Select the water molecule to begin the scene.
Activate an 'analyze' mode that highlights the lone pairs.
Trigger an animation and narration explaining that lone pairs are held only by one nucleus, occupy more space, and exert a stronger repulsive force, thus compressing the H-O-H bond angle.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the 5-domain electron geometry and show how lone pairs create seesaw, T-shaped, and linear molecular geometries. The concept of axial vs. equatorial positions is introduced.
key_visuals: A 3D model of Phosphorus Pentafluoride (PF5) representing the trigonal bipyramidal base case.
Clear labels for the two 'axial' and three 'equatorial' positions.
A note explaining that lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial positions to minimize repulsion.
student_actions: Start with the PF5 model.
Replace one equatorial bonding domain with a lone pair to form the seesaw geometry (like SF4).
Replace a second equatorial domain with a lone pair to form the T-shaped geometry (like ClF3).
Rotate the models to view their 3D shapes from all angles.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the 6-domain electron geometry and its derivatives, square pyramidal and square planar.
key_visuals: A 3D model of Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF6) representing the octahedral base case.
A model of Bromine Pentafluoride (BrF5) showing the square pyramidal shape with one lone pair.
A model of Xenon Tetrafluoride (XeF4) showing the square planar shape with two opposing lone pairs.
student_actions: Start with the SF6 model.
Replace one bonding domain with a lone pair to see the square pyramidal geometry form.
Replace the domain directly opposite the first lone pair with a second lone pair, watching the atoms settle into the square planar geometry.

scenes.brief_purpose: To assess the student's ability to apply VSEPR principles by predicting a molecule's geometry starting from its Lewis structure.
key_visuals: A virtual 2D panel displaying the Lewis structure of a target molecule (e.g., SO3 or ICl4-).
A workspace with a central atom and a palette of bonding domains and lone pair domains.
student_actions: Examine the provided Lewis structure to determine the number of bonding and lone pair domains.
Drag and drop the correct number of each type of domain onto the central atom.
Submit the constructed model to see it animate into the correct 3D geometry and receive feedback on the prediction.
